title: Tiny Snakes Cartwheel Away From Danger
paragraphs: Dwarf reed snakes, small reptiles from Southeast Asia, have an unusual way of escaping danger: they cartwheel. A new study in the journal Current Biology, led by Yosuke Kojima of Toho University in Japan, explains how this rolling works.

The researchers filmed 13 snakes from Kubah National Park in Malaysia on a narrow racetrack. All of them rolled when they were gently tapped, but six snakes from a different group, used for comparison, did not. Rolling was about four times faster than normal slithering. During each roll, one side of the body swings down to the ground, and the snake then switches sides. The head stays steady and faces forward.

The study has clear limits. Only 13 snakes were tested, and the rolling was triggered in a laboratory, so we do not know exactly how often the snakes roll in the wild. Kojima also said that the movement may need a lot of energy, but the team does not yet know how long the snakes can keep it up.

questions.q: What did the researchers do to make the snakes roll?
How much faster is rolling than slithering?
Name one limit of the study.
questions.a: Only 13 snakes were tested, or it was done in a laboratory.
